title: Analog modulation: AM, FM, PM

layers.basics: AM varies carrier amplitude, FM varies frequency, PM phase. FM resists amplitude noise.
layers.deeper: Double-sideband AM needs 2B for a message of bandwidth B. FM bandwidth is about 2(Δf + f_m), where Δf is the peak frequency deviation and f_m the highest modulating frequency (Carson’s rule, an approximation). Broadcast radio uses both.
layers.expert: Modulation index β=Δf/f_m; above its noise threshold, FM output SNR grows with β² (for tone modulation, about (3/2)β² times that of baseband transmission with the same power and noise bandwidth); envelope and quadrature detectors; SSB and VSB save bandwidth.

formula: B_FM ≈ 2(Δf + f_m), Δf = peak deviation, f_m = highest modulating frequency (Carson’s rule)

title: Digital modulation: ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM, OFDM

layers.basics: Digital modulation switches amplitude, frequency or phase between a few states; QAM mixes amplitude and phase to send many bits per symbol.
layers.deeper: A constellation plots each symbol as a point in the in-phase/quadrature plane; points that sit closer together are more easily confused by noise. OFDM sends many slow, narrow subcarriers in parallel, each carrying its own PSK or QAM symbols, so a multipath echo shorter than the guard interval does not smear one symbol into the next.
layers.expert: 16-QAM carries 4 bits/symbol; OFDM implemented with IFFT, cyclic prefix; peak-to-average power ratio problem; spectral efficiency vs SNR trade-off.

formula: bits per symbol = log₂M for an alphabet of M distinct symbols (16-QAM: 4)

title: Noise, SNR and bit error rate

layers.basics: Noise blurs received symbols; the bit error rate depends on signal-to-noise ratio and modulation type.
layers.deeper: For coherent BPSK in additive white Gaussian noise, BER = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)), where E_b is energy per bit, N₀ the noise power spectral density and Q(x) the Gaussian tail probability. Higher-order modulations need more SNR.
layers.expert: E_b/N₀ vs SNR relation SNR=(E_b/N₀)(R_b/B); Q-function tail of Gaussian; waterfall curves.

formula: BER = Q(√(2E_b/N₀)) for coherent BPSK in additive white Gaussian noise (E_b = energy per bit, N₀ = noise power spectral density, Q = Gaussian tail probability)

title: Information theory: entropy and channel capacity

layers.basics: Entropy measures information in bits; Shannon showed that every noisy channel has a capacity below which errors can be made arbitrarily small.
layers.deeper: C = B·log₂(1+S/N) bits per second for a band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise, S/N a linear power ratio (not dB) and N = N₀B. Capacity grows only logarithmically with power. With fixed signal power, widening the bandwidth also admits more noise, so capacity levels off near 1.44·S/N₀ bits per second.
layers.expert: H=−Σp log p; channel coding theorem; Shannon limit −1.59 dB on E_b/N₀ as bandwidth → ∞; turbo and LDPC codes approach it.

formula: C = B·log₂(1 + S/N) bits/s, band-limited AWGN channel, S/N a linear power ratio

layers.basics: Extra check bits let a receiver detect and fix errors; Hamming codes correct any single-bit error; CRCs detect (but do not correct) most burst and multi-bit errors.
layers.deeper: Block codes work on fixed chunks; convolutional codes work on streams, decoded with the Viterbi algorithm.
layers.expert: A code with minimum distance d_min can correct ⌊(d_min−1)/2⌋ errors or detect up to d_min−1; Reed–Solomon (QR codes, CDs); 5G NR uses LDPC codes for data channels and polar codes for control channels; coding gain.

title: Multiplexing and multiple access: FDM, TDM, CDMA, OFDMA

layers.basics: FDM gives each user a frequency slot, TDM a time slot, CDMA a code; OFDMA mixes slots in time and frequency.
layers.deeper: Mobile networks moved through them: analog 1G (AMPS) used FDMA, GSM added TDMA on top of FDMA, IS-95 and 3G WCDMA used CDMA, and 4G uses OFDMA.
layers.expert: Orthogonal codes (Walsh); processing gain=chip rate/bit rate; near–far problem; OFDMA on the LTE downlink (SC-FDMA on its uplink) and in 5G NR.

title: Wireless channels, fading and link budgets

layers.basics: Signals weaken with distance, bounce off buildings (multipath) and fade in and out as you move.
layers.deeper: A link budget works in dB: transmit power plus antenna gains minus path loss and other losses gives received power; subtracting the noise power (kTB plus the receiver noise figure) gives the received SNR.
layers.expert: Free-space path loss (4πd/λ)² between isotropic antennas in the far field; Rayleigh/Rician fading; delay spread and coherence bandwidth; Doppler; shadowing; the Friis transmission equation P_r = P_t·G_t·G_r·(λ/4πd)² and the Friis cascade formula for the noise figure of chained stages.

formula: FSPL = P_t/P_r = (4πd/λ)² between isotropic antennas in the far field (in dB: 20·log₁₀(4πd/λ)); real links add antenna gains G_t·G_r (Friis)

title: Networking basics: OSI model and TCP/IP

layers.basics: Networks are organised in layers. The OSI reference model has seven (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application). The Internet’s TCP/IP suite uses four: link, internet (IP), transport (TCP/UDP) and application; the physical layer is often drawn separately as a fifth. Each layer handles one job.
layers.deeper: Packets carry addresses; routers forward them; TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery by retransmitting lost packets; UDP just sends datagrams with no such guarantees, which suits latency-sensitive uses.
layers.expert: Ethernet/Wi-Fi at layer 2; IPv4/v6; congestion control (AIMD, BBR); NAT; TLS; bandwidth-delay product.
